problems.description: No test covers the no-op PUT (neither title nor status provided), and update tests assert only the response body — none verify a follow-up GET reflects the persisted change.
The fixture relies on importlib.reload(app_module) to pick up the monkeypatched DATABASE env var; correct for a module-level constant but fragile if imports proliferate in later sessions.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12+; pre-existing in the seed, retained rather than introduced by this commit.

strengths: Fixes a genuine correctness bug: new tasks are inserted with status 'pending' (per the story spec), not 'done'.
Removes dead code and backward-compat shims (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task) with no callers, improving maintainability without scope creep.
Adds a thorough 13-test pytest suite covering status codes (201/400/404), blank/missing title validation, created_at-desc ordering, partial updates, and cross-test persistence.
Respects the existing single-file Flask structure, get_db/init_db helpers, and update_task signature — no over-engineering in a greenfield session.
commit_reviews.summary: A disciplined greenfield session: one real bug fix (default status 'pending'), clean removal of dead code, and comprehensive Flask/pytest coverage that faithfully encodes the story spec's error-handling contract.

problems.description: require_auth reads payload["sub"] directly; a validly-signed token missing the sub claim raises KeyError → unhandled 500 instead of 401. Use payload.get("sub") and validate the type.
JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded "dev-secret-change-me" when the env var is unset — acceptable for a dev baseline but worth a startup warning or refusal outside development.

The owner_id migration (PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE) is embedded in init_db, mixing schema init with migration. Pragmatic for a single-file app, but unversioned and would grow awkwardly across further sessions.

Measured convention score of 0.70 is driven by 8 of 9 violations living in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py, test_app.py) plus a pre-existing app.py class warning; the diff itself adds no class declarations and its new code is snake_case/UPPER_CASE-consistent.

strengths: Security-aware: passwords hashed via werkzeug, expiring JWTs, strict Bearer parsing, consistent 400/401/404/201 status codes.
Correct data scoping: every task read and write filters by owner_id (including the UPDATE predicate), preventing cross-user access.
Non-destructive migration: PRAGMA-backed ALTER TABLE preserves existing tasks as unowned (NULL) rather than deleting or corrupting them.
Idiomatic Flask patterns: @wraps-preserved decorator, g.user_id context, parameterized queries, and matching section-comment structure in the existing single-file layout.
commit_reviews.summary: A strong, security-aware feature-addition commit that correctly scopes all task data to the authenticated user while respecting the app's existing single-file structure and conventions; the 0.70 mechanical convention score is dragged down by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched, and the only new debt is minor (unhandled sub-key, dev-secret fallback, unversioned migration).

problems.description: app.py imports `from notifications import send_notification_email` at module top, which instantiates the Celery app at import time — app.py now fails to import if the celery package is absent, coupling app startup to a new third-party dependency.

`send_notification_email.delay(...)` is fire-and-forget with no retry/error handling configured; if no Celery worker is running, notifications silently queue/drop with no failure signal. Operational dependency on a worker process is not documented in the module.

Discrepancy with the 0.70 mechanical score: most flagged violations are either pre-existing in untouched files (repositories.py module constants, app.py/test_app.py PascalCase — the diff adds no classes) or intentional false positives. Celery's `config_from_object` requires lowercase attribute names (`broker_url`, `result_backend`), so the UPPER_CASE flags on celery_config.py contradict the library's own convention; `celery_app`/`logger` lowercase matches both standard Python logging practice and the existing `app = Flask(__name__)` style.
The `previous is None` branch of `newly_completed` is unreachable in practice (get_task returning None implies update_task also returns None → 404), though it is defensively safe and harmless.

strengths: Comprehensive test coverage of the notification trigger: status→completed fires, non-completed and title-only updates don't, already-completed tasks don't re-trigger, and 404 paths (nonexistent / other-user's task) are covered.
Reuses existing helpers (get_task, get_user_by_id, update_task) rather than duplicating data access, keeping the edit_task integration minimal.
Env-overridable broker/backend URLs keep dev/test/prod parity without code changes; task_routes isolates the notifications queue.
The unit test uses `send_notification_email.run()` (synchronous local execution), so the suite passes without requiring a live Redis broker.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested integration of an async Celery notification on task completion that fits the existing Flask helper/controller pattern, with the low convention score driven mostly by pre-existing or library-convention false positives.

problems.description: register() now calls generate_password_hash() in the route and passes the pre-hashed value to user_repository.create(), leaking an auth/business concern into the handler layer; likewise add_task() passes datetime.utcnow().isoformat() in from the route. The repository layer pulls data access inward but pushes domain-default logic (hashing, timestamps) outward to callers, inverting part of the encapsulation the refactor claims to add.

Partial migration leaves a mixed API: module-level get_user_by_username() is retained as a compat shim while get_user_by_id/get_tasks/create_user are deleted, and repository method names are inconsistent (get_by_id vs get_by_id_and_owner, list_by_owner vs get_tasks). The shim is reasonable for migration but should be a documented short-term bridge.

BaseRepository with ABC/abstractmethod machinery may be over-engineered for only two concrete repositories, each implementing the same create/update shape; plain concrete classes (or even the existing function style) would fit the codebase's simplicity better.

Measured convention score is 0.70 (9 violations), but 6 of the 9 flagged files (celery_config.py, notifications.py, test_app.py) are untouched by this diff — the violations are pre-existing. The commit's own new code (repositories.py) is internally consistent, so I rate convention slightly above the raw measurement; flagging the discrepancy as instructed.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: all SQLite access encapsulated behind repository classes, route handlers no longer issue raw SQL
db_factory injection decouples repositories from connection management (app.get_db), making them testable
Removes the fragile dynamic-column UPDATE string (f-string column interpolation) in favor of a typed repository API
Retains a compatibility shim so existing callers/tests keep working, enabling a smooth incremental migration
Thinner, more readable route handlers after the change (+169/-92 lines, +1 file)
commit_reviews.summary: A well-motivated repository-layer refactor that cleanly separates SQL access from route handlers and removes fragile dynamic SQL, though it mildly over-engineers with ABC machinery and leaks password-hashing/timestamps into the route layer.

problems.description: count_by_owner() runs a COUNT(*) on every page fetch; on large task tables this doubles the query cost per request.
next_cursor is emitted whenever len(tasks) == limit, including on the final page, so a client fetches one trailing empty page before seeing null.
GET /tasks response shape changed from a bare list to {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking contract change for any existing consumer.
Ordering silently switched from created_at DESC to id DESC; equivalent only while ids are insertion-ordered, and the ordering test still passes for that reason.

strengths: Keyset (cursor) pagination over offset pagination — stable under insert churn and scales without OFFSET cost.
Per-user rate-limit key with IP fallback for unauthenticated endpoints — the auth boundary is handled correctly, not naively.
Thorough test coverage: default limit, limit param, 100 cap, cursor paging, plus fakeredis isolation so tests need no real Redis and don't leak limiter state.
Limit is clamped to [1, 100] server-side, and repository methods follow the existing BaseRepository/_fetchall pattern exactly.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid cross-cutting commit — rate limiting and keyset pagination follow the existing repository and test patterns with strong coverage; the 0.70 convention score is dragged down almost entirely by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py), not by anything this diff adds (+0 new classes, all new functions snake_case).

compounding_issues: Single-file seed constrained sessions 1-2: JWT auth was crammed into app.py (146->~230 lines), inflating the monolith until session 4's repository refactor paid the structural debt down

Infrastructure coupling accumulated: session 3 introduced Celery/Redis for async notifications, then session 5 added Flask-Limiter on the same Redis broker, both defaulting to localhost:6379 — the app now hard-requires Redis at runtime, with tests papering over it via fakeredis monkeypatching

Monotonic scope/complexity growth drove a cost blowup at the end: session 5 (cross-cutting) cost $1.85 vs $0.26-0.66 for sessions 1-4, used 31K tokens (~3-8x prior), 45 tool calls, 7 retries, 355s, and confidence fell to 0.667 — the accumulated auth+ownership+repository layers made the final change set the hardest
JWT_SECRET default ('dev-secret-change-me') and permissive env config left a security-posture placeholder that never got hardened across the sessions
key_decisions: Session 2: JWT auth with per-user task ownership (owner_id) — established the multi-tenant permission model that sessions 3-5 all depend on (email owner notification, per-user rate limiting, per-owner pagination)
Session 2: idempotent in-place schema migration (ALTER TABLE guard in init_db) — kept the seed database and existing rows working across session boundaries, critical for multi-session continuity

Session 3: async email notifications via Celery + Redis with a mocked transport (notifications.py, celery_config.py) — first module split from the monolith and the introduction of queue infrastructure

Session 4: Repository pattern refactor (BaseRepository ABC, UserRepository/TaskRepository) extracting all SQL out of routes — the cleanest architectural move; directly enabled session 5's paginated list_by_owner_page/count_by_owner
Session 5: user-keyed rate limiting (Flask-Limiter with Redis storage, IP fallback for anonymous) + cursor-based pagination layered on the repository abstraction
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved and consolidated across a textbook arc: session 1 (greenfield) was fast, cheap, and high-confidence; session 2 (JWT auth/ownership) added the security and multi-tenancy model cheaply; session 3 (async notifications) introduced Celery/Redis infrastructure at modest cost; session 4 (repository refactor) was the debt-payoff structural upgrade — confidence dipped to 0.7 with 3 retries as it rewired the whole data layer, but it succeeded and became the foundation for the finale; session 5 (rate limiting + pagination) was by far the hardest and most expensive (7 retries, 45 tool calls, 0.667 confidence) yet it landed cleanly. Test coverage grew monotonically (13 -> 31 -> 39 -> 39 -> 51 tests, test_code_ratio 1.31) with all suites green (test_executed_success=true). The system became architecturally stronger and better-tested each session, but at sharply increasing marginal cost as complexity compounded.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session progression — greenfield, auth/ownership, async integration, repository refactor, cross-cutting hardening — that improved architecture and test coverage monotonically while a final, complexity-compounded cross-cutting session absorbed the bulk of the cost and effort.
